Stars form inside cold molecular clouds made mostly of hydrogen, helium, and microscopic dust grains.
Small density differences let gravity gather material into knots, while turbulence and magnetic fields resist collapse.
When one knot becomes dense enough, its centre contracts into a protostar surrounded by a rotating disk.
The contracting gas converts gravitational energy into heat, so the young object's core grows steadily hotter.
Jets launched along the rotation axis carry away angular momentum and clear channels through the surrounding cloud.
Material continues to fall from the disk onto the protostar, increasing both its mass and its internal pressure.
Once the core reaches roughly ten million kelvin, hydrogen nuclei begin fusing into helium through nuclear reactions.
Fusion releases energy that pushes outward, balancing the inward pull of gravity in a state called hydrostatic equilibrium.
At that point the object has entered the main sequence, the long stable phase that occupies most of a star's life.
The star's mass determines its temperature, brightness, fuel consumption, and eventual path after the main sequence.
